power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background and objectives: Animal-assisted interventions have been introduced in adolescent mental health care, but evidence for their added benefit in inpatient treatment remains limited.
This study examined animal-assisted group psychotherapy across three assessment intervals: 1) the individual sessions, 2) the five-week intervention period, 3) the full inpatient stay.
Methods: This controlled study included 276 adolescents aged 12-18 years receiving inpatient psychosomatic treatment.

The intervention group (n = 108) participated in five weekly 150-minute animal-assisted group psychotherapy sessions alongside standard multimodal treatment, whereas the control group (n = 168) received standard treatment alone.
Group allocation was determined by the treating clinicians based on predefined clinical indications and safety criteria.

Linear mixed-effects models examined 1) immediate pre-post session changes in depressive symptoms and mindfulness, 2) change in depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness across the intervention period, and 3) admission-to-discharge changes in depressive symptoms by group.
Results: Depressive symptoms decreased (b = -2.53 to -3.04, all p < .001) and mindfulness increased (b = 4.88 to 6.36, all p ≤ .001) immediately after individual sessions.
text.formatted: Results: Depressive symptoms decreased (b = -2.53 to -3.04, all p < .001) and mindfulness increased (b = 4.88 to 6.36, all p ≤ .001) immediately after individual sessions.

text.text: Across the intervention period, depressive symptoms decreased, while self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness increased significantly (all p ≤ .031).

Although depressive symptoms decreased substantially from admission to discharge in both groups, no significant time × group interactions were found for the BDI-II (b = 1.36, p = .371) or PHQ-9 (b = 0.65, p = .394).

The findings suggest that animal-assisted group psychotherapy may provide short-term psychological benefits for adolescents receiving inpatient mental health care, potentially supporting readiness, attention, and therapeutic engagement.
However, these immediate benefits do not necessarily translate into additional improvements in depressive symptoms over the course of inpatient treatment.

Globally, approximately one in seven adolescents aged 10-19 years experiences a mental disorder, with depression among the leading causes of illness and disability during this developmental period (World Health Organization, 2025).

text.text: Many mental disorders first emerge during adolescence or early adulthood and approximately half of all lifetime mental disorders have their onset before the age of 20, highlighting the importance of early detection and therapeutic interventions (McGrath et al., 2023; Solmi et al., 2022).

text.text: Although evidence-based psychological and pharmacological treatments are available, not all adolescents respond sufficiently, and maintaining engagement and motivation can be challenging, particularly during intensive inpatient treatment.
Consequently, there is growing interest in complementary approaches that can be integrated into established treatment programs.

Treatment of adolescents with mental health disorders aims not only to reduce psychological symptoms but also to strengthen positive aspects of psychological functioning, including selfconcept and self-esteem.

Self-concept refers to the organized, multifaceted, and hierarchical system of perceptions individuals hold about themselves, whereas self-esteem represents the evaluative dimension of the self, particularly an individual's subjective evaluation of his or her worth as a person (Donnellan et al., 2011; Shavelson et al., 1976).

text.text: Both undergo substantial development during adolescence and are closely related to depressive symptoms (Hards et al., 2020; Orchard et al., 2021; Van Der Cruijsen et al., 2023).

text.text: Given their relevance to adolescent psychological functioning, selfconcept and self-esteem represent important outcomes when evaluating interventions for adolescents with mental health disorders.
Mindfulness is another relevant aspect of psychological functioning in adolescence.

It is commonly conceptualized as the regulation of attention toward present-moment experience, thereby increasing awareness of mental processes and supporting more skillful responses to emotional distress and maladaptive behavior (Bishop et al., 2004).

text.text: In a clinical adolescent sample, mindfulness-based treatment has been associated with reductions in anxiety, depressive, and somatization symptoms, and improved self-esteem (Biegel et al., 2009).

text.text: Together, depressive symptoms, selfesteem, self-concept, and mindfulness capture both psychopathological symptoms and positive aspects of psychological functioning.

Their combined assessment is consistent with models proposing that adolescent mental health should be evaluated using both negative indicators of psychopathology and positive indicators of psychological functioning (Magalhães, 2024) Animal-assisted interventions represent one complementary approach that may be beneficial in strengthening these symptom-and resource-oriented outcomes.

text.text: Animal-assisted intervention is an umbrella term for structured, goal-oriented interventions that intentionally incorporate animals into therapeutic, educational, or human services.

Within this framework, animal-assisted therapy (AAT) refers specifically to planned and documented interventions delivered by qualified health or humanservice professionals as part of their clinical practice (International Association of Human-Animal Interaction Organizations, 2018).

text.text: Integrating animals into psychotherapy may offer additional opportunities for therapeutic engagement and experiential learning (Jones et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2017).

text.text: Through their responses to human behavior and nonverbal cues, animals may provide feedback that helps adolescents become more aware of their own emotional and behavioral responses (Pendry et al., 2018).

text.text: Interacting with animals may provide opportunities for adolescents to experience competence and develop confidence and assertiveness, potentially contributing to positive self-esteem (Shen et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2017).

text.text: Furthermore, positive interactions with animals may also provide calming experiences that facilitate engagement in therapeutic activities (Jones et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2018).

text.text: Systematic reviews suggest potential benefits for psychopathological symptoms, emotional well-being, and social and behavioral functioning among children and adolescents with mental health difficulties (Hoagwood et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2019).

text.text: More specific evidence from controlled studies suggests that canine-and equine-assisted interventions can have beneficial effects in children and adolescents, although research examining these interventions among inpatient populations with significant mental health needs remains relatively scarce.

Two small randomized controlled trials examined canine-assisted therapy as an adjunct to standard inpatient psychiatric care. Stefanini et al. text.text: Taken together, previous studies provide preliminary evidence that animal-assisted interventions may improve internalizing symptoms in adolescents.
However, findings remain mixed, particularly for depression, self-esteem and other self-related outcomes.
Several methodological limitations may contribute to these inconsistent findings.

The existing evidence is limited by small samples in populations characterized by mental health symptoms varying in type, severity and progression, which increases the risk of Type II error and may contribute to nonsignificant findings.
Medication use has rarely been considered adequately, despite its potential influence on psychological symptoms.
Furthermore, studies have often relied on single or broad measures of internalizing symptoms or those associated with depression rather than comprehensive assessments of depression.
Most have also focused on simple pre-post comparisons, without distinguishing changes across individual therapy sessions, the intervention period, and the full inpatient stay.

This distinction is important because treatment effects may develop through stepwise changes across different time frames, beginning with immediate responses within individual sessions and extending to broader changes across the intervention and treatment periods.
The present study addresses these limitations in several ways.
The comparatively large sample provides greater statistical power to detect intervention effects, while matching based on medication helps reduce potential confounding.

The study simultaneously assesses depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness, with depression measured using multiple validated instruments to provide a more comprehensive assessment of symptom severity and change.
Finally, in our study we examine changes across three distinct assessment intervals: (1) individual therapy sessions, (2) the intervention period, and (3) the full inpatient stay.

This approach captures immediate session-level changes, assesses changes across the five-week intervention period within the intervention group, and compares admission-to-discharge changes in depressive symptoms between the intervention and control groups.
Assessing outcomes across different assessment intervals helps distinguish immediate changes following individual sessions from broader changes.
Accordingly, the study addressed three research questions: 1.
Research Question (RQ1): Do depressive symptoms and mindfulness change from before to after individual AAT sessions, and do these changes vary across sessions?
Research Question (RQ2): How do depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness change across the intervention period within the intervention group?
Research Question (RQ3): Do changes in depressive symptoms across the full inpatient stay differ between the intervention and control groups?

We expected improvements in depressive symptoms and mindfulness immediately following individual sessions (H1), as well as improvements in depressive symptoms, self-esteem, selfconcept, and mindfulness across the five-week intervention period (H2).

We further hypothesized that reductions in depressive symptoms from admission to discharge would be greater among adolescents receiving animal-assisted group psychotherapy in addition to standard inpatient treatment than among those receiving standard treatment alone (H3).
Differences in immediate changes across sessions were examined exploratorily.
The study used a nonrandomized controlled design with clinician-determined group allocation.
Participants were recruited among adolescents receiving inpatient psychosomatic treatment at Schön Klinik Bad Arolsen, Germany, between March and November 2021.
No prospective sample-size calculation was performed.
The sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients recruited during the study period for whom the required outcome data were available.
The initial sample comprised 279 patients.

Three patients from the intervention group were excluded from the analyses because of extensive missing data or the absence of intervention-related data, resulting in a final sample of 276 adolescents (intervention group: n = 108; control group: n = 168).

General inclusion criteria were an age of 12-18 years at the start of treatment, informed parental consent, sufficient German language proficiency, and a clinical diagnosis of a mental health disorder, specifically major depressive episode, eating disorder, anxiety disorder, and/or obsessivecompulsive disorder, according to the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10; World Health Organization, 2004).
text.formatted: General inclusion criteria were an age of 12-18 years at the start of treatment, informed parental consent, sufficient German language proficiency, and a clinical diagnosis of a mental health disorder, specifically major depressive episode, eating disorder, anxiety disorder, and/or obsessivecompulsive disorder, according to the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision <ref type="bibr">(ICD-10;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Health Organization, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: While the registered study protocol specified an upper age limit of 17 years, it was extended to 18 years to reflect the age range of patients treated at the clinic.

General exclusion criteria included acute suicidality, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, substance use disorder, organic mental disorder, a current Axis I disorder other than the primary diagnosis, severe physical illness, insufficient physical fitness due to anorexia nervosa, and the need for ongoing therapeutically supervised meals within the clinic.
The individual patient was the unit of allocation.

Treating psychotherapists and physicians determined eligibility for AAT according to predefined clinical indications, including promoting mindfulness and self-awareness; enhancing self-esteem and self-efficacy; developing assertiveness and boundary-setting skills; addressing self-image and identity; increasing activation; and strengthening treatment engagement.
Patients were excluded from AAT if they exhibited pronounced emotional instability, had a fear of animals, or had animal allergies.
Before enrollment, clinicians assessed each patient's physical health and emotional stability to determine suitability for participation in group therapy sessions held outside the clinic.
Particular attention was given to the physical health of patients with eating disorders.
These assessments were conducted in consultation with the head physician and/or the responsible ward physician.
The control group comprised patients treated during the same period who met the general eligibility criteria but did not participate in AAT.
Antidepressant medication status was used as a stratification factor to obtain comparable proportions of medicated and unmedicated patients in the two groups.
Before participation, patients and their legal guardians provided written informed consent.

Both groups received standard inpatient treatment, including pharmacotherapy, group therapy, sports therapy, art therapy, supervised group meals, mindfulness-based therapy, and other therapeutic services.
The intervention group additionally participated in a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program.
During the corresponding time slots, the control group received no additional therapy.
All patients completed a routine depression assessment at admission (T0) and discharge (T3).

Participants in the intervention group completed additional measures at the beginning (T1) and end (T2) of the five-week intervention and brief assessments immediately before (S1) and after (S2) each therapy session (see Figure 1).

The study protocol complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable German legal and regulatory requirements.
The study was registered in the Dutch Trial Register and is available via the https://www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/19949.

All research methods complied with the relevant ethical and regulatory guidelines, and the study is reported in accordance with the Transparent Reporting of Evaluations with Nonrandomized Designs (TREND) statement.

The animal-assisted group psychotherapy was conducted by a child and adolescent psychotherapist in training, who was simultaneously completing a certified program in AAT at an institute accredited by the International Society for Animal Assisted Therapy (ISAAT; https://isaat.org/).

text.text: The intervention was supported through regular consultation and supervision by a senior physician and the project's medical director.
This included ongoing monitoring to ensure adherence to the treatment manual.
The intervention manual was developed based on established group psychotherapy protocols used at Schön Klinik Bad Arolsen and grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy.
All hygiene procedures related to animal contact and therapy sessions were implemented in accordance with the clinic's institutional standards.
The intervention also complied with the guidelines of the
Veterinary Association for Animal Welfare (Tierärztliche Vereinigung für Tierschutz, TVT).

The psychotherapy program aimed to use the potential anxiety-reducing, activating, and antidepressant effects of animal interactions to stabilize and improve patients' mood, enhance intrinsic motivation, promote mindfulness, and strengthen self-efficacy.
The program comprised five weekly group sessions of 150 minutes each, conducted on the farm of the therapist delivering the intervention.
Groups included a maximum of seven participants, and no minimum group size was required.
Each session combined theoretical discussion, practical exercises with dogs and horses, and guided reflection.
The theoretical components addressed human-animal relationships, mindfulness, non-verbal communication, body language, personal boundaries, and relationship experiences.
During the practical components, participants completed progressively structured exercises involving observation, communication, mindful leading, and direct interaction with the animals.
For example, participants practiced guiding dogs and horses through deliberate body language while peers observed and described their behavior.
The therapist provided individualized guidance, and participants reflected on how their posture, communication, and relational behavior influenced the animals and the interaction.

Across sessions, the exercises progressed from becoming familiar with the animals and observing non-verbal communication to practicing mindful leadership, reflecting on relationships, and integrating the acquired skills during a group walk.

text.text: The therapy program involved both dogs and horses (including ponies).
Six therapy dogs participated in the program.
Four belonged to the therapist and lived on the farm, while two belonged to a staff member working there and were present on most days.
The dogs were a mix of breeds, including Hovawart/Bernese/Sheepdog, Labrador/Golden Retriever, Samoyed, Labrador mix, and Terrier mix.
Ages ranged from 4 to 11 years.
Three of the dogs were female (two intact, one neutered), and three were male (two intact, one neutered).
All dogs were raised in a group setting, forming a social hierarchy that allowed each to develop a distinct personality.
This diversity enabled each patient to connect with a dog that suited their individual needs.
All dogs were trained by the therapist and assessed for therapeutic suitability by a veterinarian.
Additionally, three horses and two ponies lived on the farm in a large, natural open stable.
The horses included an English Warmblood mare, a Zweibrücker mare, and a Haflinger-Quarter-mix gelding, aged between 10 and 22 years.
The ponies were Shetland mares aged 4 and 5 years.
To ensure animal welfare, all sessions were accompanied by a certified animal welfare practitioner.
Animal participation was entirely voluntary; dogs, horses, and ponies were free to leave the sessions at any time.

text.text: In the registered study protocol, the BDI-II and PHQ-9 were designated as primary outcomes, whereas all other measures were designated as secondary outcomes.
The BDI-II is a 21-item self-report measure of cognitive, affective, somatic, and vegetative symptoms of depression in adolescents and adults.
Items are rated from 0 to 3, yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 63, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.
Scores of 0-13 indicate minimal, 14-19 mild, 20-28 moderate, and 29-63 severe depressive symptoms.
The BDI-II has demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .91) and validity (A. T. Beck et al., 1996).
text.formatted: The BDI-II has demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .91) and validity (A. T. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Beck et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The PHQ-9 is the nine-item depression module of the Patient Health Questionnaire and assesses the frequency of depressive symptoms during the previous two weeks.
Items are rated from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 27.
Scores of 0-4 indicate minimal, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, and 20-27 severe depressive symptoms.
A score of 10 or higher is commonly used to indicate clinically relevant depressive symptoms.
The PHQ-9 has demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = .89) and validity (Kroenke et al., 2001).

text.text: The Beck Depression Inventory for Youth (BDI-Y) is a 20-item self-report scale assessing affective, cognitive, and motivational symptoms of depression in children and adolescents aged 7-18 years.
Items are rated from 0 (never) to 3 (always) and summed to obtain a total score ranging from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating greater depressive symptom severity.
Age-based normative data permit the interpretation of individual scores relative to clinically meaningful ranges.
The BDI-Y has demonstrated excellent internal consistency in adolescents (α = .90-.94) and convergent and discriminant validity (J. S. Beck et al., 2019).

text.text: The ADS-L is a 20-item self-report measure of affective, cognitive, somatic, and behavioral symptoms of depression during the previous week.
Items are rated from 0 (rarely or never) to 3 (most or all of the time), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 60.
Higher scores indicate greater depressive symptom severity, and a score of 23 or higher is commonly used to indicate clinically relevant symptoms.
The ADS-L has demonstrated good internal consistency (α = .82-.88) and validity in clinical and research settings (Hautzinger et al., 2012).

text.text: The MSWS comprises 32 items across six subscales: emotional self-esteem (ESWS), social self-esteem related to interpersonal contact (SWKO), social self-esteem related to criticism (SWKR), performance-related self-esteem (LSWS), perceived physical attractiveness (SWPA), and perceived athletic competence (SWSP).
Items are rated on seven-point scales, with higher scores indicating higher self-esteem.
All scale scores were calculated as mean scores (ranging from 1.00 and 7.00), with higher scores indicating higher levels of selfesteem.
The higher-order Social Self-Esteem scale (SSW) was calculated by combining the items from the SWKO and SWKR subscales.
The higher-order Body-Related Self-Esteem (KSW) was calculated by combining the items from the SWPA and SWSP subscales.
In the present sample, internal consistency ranged from α = .76 to .93 at T1 and from α = .79 to .93 at T2, indicating acceptable to excellent reliability.
Self-concept was assessed at T1 and T2 using the Beck Self-Concept Inventory for Youth (BSCI-Y) from the BYI-2 (J. S. Beck et al., 2019).

text.text: The BSCI-Y comprises 20 items assessing positive self-perceptions, such as pride, competence, and perceived personal strengths.
Items are rated from 0 (never) to 3 (always), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 60 with higher total scores indicating a more positive self-concept.
The scale has demonstrated good internal consistency in adolescents (α = .81-.87) and convergent and discriminant validity (J. S. Beck et al., 2019).

text.text: The 30-item FFA assesses mindful awareness and acceptance of presentmoment experiences, including attention to current experience, nonjudgmental acceptance, and openness toward internal states.
Items are rated on a scale from 1 (rarely) to 4 (almost always), yielding a total score ranging from 30 to 120, with higher total scores indicating greater mindfulness.
The scale has demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = .93) and construct validity in both meditating and nonmeditating samples (Walach et al., 2006).

text.text: All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025).
Model assumptions were evaluated graphically using residual-versus-fitted plots, scale-location plots, and normal Q-Q plots of the conditional residuals.
No substantial violations of the model assumptions were identified.
All models converged without warnings and showed no evidence of singularity.
Outliers were assessed using both Z-score transformation (|z| > 3.00) and visual inspection of boxplots.
text.formatted: Outliers were assessed using both Z-score transformation (|z| > 3.00) and visual inspection of boxplots.

text.text: Only a very small proportion of data points were identified as outliers (0.24% using the Zscore criterion and 1.08% using the boxplot/IQR criterion).
As all identified values fell within the expected and interpretable range of the respective questionnaire scales, no observations were excluded or modified.
Missing item-level responses occurred only in the MSWS.
For this questionnaire, missing responses were replaced using person-mean imputation when at least 50% of the items within the respective scale were available.
Overall, 0.4% of MSWS item-level responses were imputed.
The individual patient was the unit of analysis.
Repeated measurements were nested within patients and accounted for using linear mixed-effects models fitted with the lmer() function from the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Repeated measurements were nested within patients and accounted for using linear mixed-effects models fitted with the lmer() function from the lme4 package <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood.
Separate models were fitted for each outcome.
Primary analyses were conducted following the intention-to-treat principle, with participants analyzed in their assigned condition regardless of intervention attendance.

In addition, sensitivity analyses were performed including only participants who attended at least three animal-assisted group psychotherapy sessions to assess whether the findings remained consistent after excluding participants with only limited intervention exposure.
To examine immediate changes in depressive symptoms and mindfulness within individual AAT sessions (RQ1), separate linear mixed-effects models were estimated for each outcome.
Fixed effects included within-session assessment point (pre-session vs. post-session), session number (sessions 1-5, reference session 1), and their interaction.
The interaction tested whether the magnitude of the within-session pre-post change differed across sessions.
Session number was modelled as a categorical factor, allowing a separate pre-post difference to be estimated for each session without assuming a linear trend across sessions.
Primary models adjusted for age and gender, and sensitivity models additionally adjusted for length of clinic stay.
Random intercepts were specified for participants and for sessions nested within participants to account for repeated sessions and the dependence between the pre-and post-session assessments.
Estimated marginal means were calculated using the emmeans package (Lenth, 2024), and pre-post contrasts were estimated separately for each session.
text.formatted: Estimated marginal means were calculated using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Lenth, 2024)</ref>, and pre-post contrasts were estimated separately for each session.

text.text: The resulting p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni method across the five session-specific pre-post contrasts for each outcome.

To examine changes in depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness across the intervention period (RQ2), separate linear mixed-effects models were estimated within the intervention group.
Assessment time (pre-intervention vs. post-intervention) was included as a fixed effect, and a participant-specific random intercept accounted for repeated observations.
Primary models adjusted for age and gender, and sensitivity models additionally adjusted for length of clinic stay.
Exploratory models included the number of sessions attended and its interaction with assessment time to examine whether pre-post changes were associated with intervention attendance.
None of the primary models showed a singular fit, and intraclass correlations ranged from .69 to .89, supporting participant-specific random intercepts.
To compare changes in depressive symptoms across the full inpatient stay (RQ3), separate linear mixed-effects models were estimated for the BDI-II and PHQ-9.
Fixed effects included assessment time (clinic admission vs. discharge), group (intervention vs. control), and the time × group interaction.
Primary models adjusted for age and gender, and sensitivity models additionally adjusted for length of clinic stay.
Additional exploratory models replaced group with the total number of AAT sessions attended, coded as zero for control participants.
These models included assessment time, number of sessions attended, and their interaction and adjusted for age and gender.
The assessment time × session attendance interaction tested whether admission-to-discharge changes in depressive symptoms were associated with the number of sessions attended.
Unstandardized model coefficients (𝑏𝑏) were used as effect-size estimates and are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
The significance level was set at 𝛼𝛼 = .05.

text.text: The present study examined outcomes associated with a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program delivered alongside standard multimodal inpatient treatment for adolescents with mental health disorders across three assessment intervals.

The first hypothesis, which predicted immediate decreases in depressive symptoms and increases in mindfulness from pre-to post-session, was supported, with significant changes observed in all five sessions.

The second hypothesis, which predicted decreases in depressive symptoms and increases in self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness across the intervention period of five weeks within the intervention group, was also supported.
Hypothesis 3, which predicted greater admission-to-discharge reductions in depressive symptoms in the intervention group than in the control group, was not supported.

Thus, the changes observed during individual sessions and across the intervention period were not reflected in a detectable additional reduction in depressive symptoms relative to standard inpatient treatment alone.
The session-level findings provide the most direct insight into adolescents' immediate responses to individual AAT sessions.
Depressive symptoms decreased and mindfulness increased from pre-to post-session in each of the five sessions.
The repeated reductions in depressive symptoms and increases in mindfulness across the sessions suggest a relatively consistent pattern of short-term change associated with session participation.

The reductions in depressive symptoms converge with previous studies reporting immediate improvements in mood and reductions in subjective distress following therapy-dog activities in psychiatric and pediatric behavioral-health settings (Brown et al., 2020; Fodstad et al., 2019).

text.text: However, these earlier studies did not examine session-specific changes across a standardized multi-session intervention.
The present study extends this evidence by repeatedly assessing depressive symptoms before and after five structured therapy sessions in a clinical adolescent sample.

The immediate increases in mindfulness represent a particularly novel finding. Trujillo et al. (2020) incorporated a therapy dog into mindfulness and communication exercises for adolescents with psychiatric and substance use disorders.

text.text: However, that study assessed treatment attendance, school engagement, and general well-being rather than mindfulness itself.
Similarly, Künzi et al. (2022) evaluated animal-assisted psychotherapy incorporating mindfulness and self-compassion among adults undergoing neurorehabilitation.

text.text: Although mindfulness itself was not assessed as an outcome, participants in the animal-assisted condition showed greater immediate improvements in several emotional states, including feeling secure, accepted, motivated, and at ease, than those receiving the same intervention without animal assistance.
Direct evidence regarding changes in mindfulness has mainly been obtained from adults with recurrent depression.
In a small pilot study, Schramm et al. (2015) reported improvements in overall mindfulness skills following nature-and animal-assisted mindfulness training.

text.text: However, a subsequent randomized trial found benefits for relapse prevention but no additional improvements in mindfulness compared with usual care (Schramm et al., 2022).

text.text: The present findings therefore provide direct evidence that mindfulness may increase immediately following AAT sessions among adolescents.
Several processes might contribute to these immediate changes.
Animals may direct attention toward sensory, emotional, and relational cues and provide nonverbal feedback to adolescents' behavior, body language, and emotional state.
The experiential nature of the sessions may therefore temporarily interrupt maladaptive thought patterns and facilitate greater engagement with presentmoment experience.
Such proximal changes may be clinically relevant if they increase emotional readiness, motivation, or engagement in subsequent therapeutic activities.
Consistent with our second hypothesis, the intervention group showed significant improvements across several psychological outcomes over the five-week intervention period.
Depressive symptoms decreased, while self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness increased.

The reductions in depressive symptoms are consistent with previous controlled studies. Frederick et al. (2015) found greater reductions in depression following a five-week equine-assisted learning program than following treatment as usual among at-risk adolescents. Muela et al. (2017) similarly reported greater reductions in depression and sense of inadequacy among adolescents receiving animal-assisted psychotherapy compared with those receiving usual residential care without AAT.

text.text: The present findings extend this literature to adolescents receiving intensive inpatient psychiatric treatment, a novel finding.

Our findings supporting improvements in self-esteem and self-concept add to a limited and mixed evidence base. Trotter et al. (2008) reported significantly greater improvements in self-esteem among at-risk youths receiving equine-assisted counseling than among those receiving classroombased counseling.

text.text: More recently, Rodrigo-Claverol et al. (2026) compared a structured therapeutic activity conducted with a therapy dog with the corresponding activity conducted without a dog among adolescent psychiatric inpatients.
The animal-assisted group showed a small but significantly greater improvement in self-efficacy.
Although self-efficacy is conceptually distinct from self-esteem and self-concept, this finding provides related evidence that AAT may support adolescents' perceptions of their own competence.

The improvements across multiple dimensions of self-esteem and self-concept are clinically relevant because negative self-evaluation is closely associated with adolescent depression and may contribute to its persistence (Hards et al., 2020; Orchard et al., 2021).

text.text: The intervention in this study included experiential exercises involving communication, body language, boundary setting, and guiding animals.
Successfully interacting with or influencing an animal may provide concrete experiences of competence, agency, and self-efficacy, which could contribute to more positive selfevaluations.

An important contribution of the present study is the simultaneous assessment of depressive symptoms, multidimensional self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness, which provides a broader picture of changes during the intervention than studies focusing only on general symptoms or functioning.

Depressive symptoms decreased substantially from admission to discharge in both groups, but, contrary to our third hypothesis, the improvement was not significantly greater in the intervention group than in the control group.
Thus, the controlled comparison provided no evidence that animalassisted group psychotherapy produced additional improvement in depressive symptoms beyond standard inpatient treatment.
This finding should be considered within the context of the intensive multimodal treatment received by both groups.

Moreover, the admission-to-discharge assessments captured overall changes in depressive symptoms across the entire inpatient stay, potentially obscuring short-term improvements associated with individual AAT sessions.

Reporting these nonsignificant findings contributes to a more balanced understanding of the potential benefits and limitations of AAT and strengthens the broader evidence base, particularly given the methodological rigor of the present study.
The absence of an additional effect on depressive symptoms is consistent with the mixed evidence concerning small sample studies on animal-assisted interventions.

Small randomized studies involving child and adolescent psychiatric inpatients have reported improvements in internalizing symptoms, competence, and global functioning following animal-assisted therapy compared with standard treatment (Stefanini et al., 2015 (Stefanini et al., , 2016)).

text.text: The findings are not necessarily contradictory: AAT may be associated with improvements in broader aspects of functioning or internalizing symptoms without an additional effect on depressive symptoms specifically.
The absence of an overall additional effect may also indicate that not all adolescents benefit equally.
Future research is needed to identify which patients are most likely to benefit from AAT as an adjunct to standard care.
The study has several strengths.
Its comparatively large clinical sample allowed intervention outcomes to be examined with greater precision than in many previous animal-assisted intervention studies.
Conducting the study in a naturalistic inpatient setting enhanced its clinical relevance.
Efforts to balance the intervention and control groups with respect to antidepressant medication use helped reduce potential medication-related confounding.
Multiple validated measures of depression were used, and depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness were assessed simultaneously during the intervention period.
This enabled the examination of both psychopathological symptoms and positive psychological resources.

The study combined a comparison-group analysis across the full inpatient stay with repeated within-intervention-group assessments across the five-week intervention period and individual therapy sessions.
In particular, the session-level assessments provided information about immediate changes that would have been obscured by relying solely on admission and discharge assessments.
Finally, the intention-to-treat analyses and sensitivity analyses based on intervention attendance generally supported the robustness of the main findings.
Several limitations must also be considered.
First, participants were not randomly assigned to conditions.
This approach was chosen to ensure that the intervention was clinically relevant and could be delivered safely within routine inpatient care.
Although it strengthens the ecological validity of the study, it creates a risk of selection bias and confounding by indication.
The comparable baseline levels of depressive symptoms and the balancing of antidepressant medication use across conditions may reduce this concern.
Second, although validated self-report instruments and standardized assessment procedures supported data quality, responses may have been influenced by treatment expectations.
Including clinician ratings, behavioral observations, or physiological indicators of stress would provide a more comprehensive assessment.
Third, generalizability may be limited by the single-site, predominantly female inpatient sample and the specific farm-based intervention.
The findings may therefore not apply to other populations, settings, or intervention formats, and the absence of follow-up precludes conclusions about longer-term effects.

AAT may support proximal therapeutic processes, with immediate reductions in depressive symptoms and increases in mindfulness potentially facilitating adolescents' readiness and engagement in subsequent therapeutic activities, particularly among those who initially struggle to engage in conventional psychotherapy.
Clinically, this study suggests that AAT sessions could be scheduled before demanding individual or group interventions.

This work also demonstrates that repeated session-level assessments may capture changes overlooked by conventional pre-post designs and as such could be incorporated into treatment and assessment protocols.

That said, although AAT was associated with improvements in depressive symptoms, self-esteem, self-concept, and mindfulness across the intervention period, it did not yield significantly greater reductions in depressive symptoms from admission to discharge than standard inpatient treatment.
These findings suggest that AAT's benefits may be most evident at the session level rather than in overall treatment outcomes.
Future randomized controlled trials with these understudied inpatient populations are needed to strengthen causal inference.
